item.title: I asked Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6, and Grok 4.6 to copy the same polished UI — tiny details exposed the winner
item.itunes:title: I asked Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6, and Grok 4.6 to copy the same polished UI — tiny details exposed the winner
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Building a simple webpage with AI isn’t hard anymore, but making it look polished and intentional is a different story. It’s easy for a model to generate working code; it’s much harder for it to balance margins, pick the right contrast, and keep every visual element aligned.

I wanted to find out which flagship tool has the best eye for design, so I tasked Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6, and Grok 4.6 with the exact same website interface. While all three produced something functional, the tiny details immediately separated the average results from the truly impressive ones.

Claude Code's creator keeps sharing tips, and they all made my experience better

Who better to learn from than the person who built it?

By  Mahnoor Faisal

A word on the prompt

And my preferred IDEs

To put each model to its limits, I skipped vague prompts and put together an end-to-end design brief: building a full-stack, production-ready e-commerce product page for a fictional high-end audio brand called Auralis.

The prompt left zero room for shortcuts. It demanded strict brand guidelines, custom color palettes, exact layout ratios, interactive elements, and full mobile responsiveness using React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS.

To keep the playing field realistic, I ran this prompt directly inside each model’s native environment: Claude Opus 5 in Claude, GPT-5.6 in ChatGPT, and Grok 4.6 in Cursor.

GPT-5.6

Functional at first glance, but flawed in the fine details

At first glance, GPT-5.6 seemed to hit a home run. It generated a complete, working React component on the very first try without throwing syntax errors or choking on the brief. The layout structure matched the requirement, the color palette felt polished, and the main hero section looked reasonably well put together.

But the moment I loaded the preview and started actually using the page, the issues in its design choices began to show. The most obvious problem was the typography scaling. For some reason, GPT-5.6 has a recurring habit across all my testing of making body text and secondary labels way too small.

Things got worse once I started interacting with the components. The technical specification menu was poorly designed. Instead of giving each spec item its own distinct detail, it recycled the same generic copy across multiple sections.

The ‘You may also like’ section also felt like an afterthought. The proportions were awkward, image placeholders lacked visual balance, and the cards lacked refined spacing. The footer was needlessly massive. GPT-5.6 proved it can follow instructions and spit out functional code fast, but its default eye aesthetic balance left a lot to be desired.

Grok 4.6

Blazing speed and sharp typography with minor UX stumbles

Running Grok 4.6 inside Cursor was an impressive experience right out of the gate. The speed is excellent, and it nailed the typography from the jump. Font sizing, line heights, and letter-spacing across the hero and feature sections felt deliberate, readable, and scaled for a luxury audio brand.

That said, it wasn’t a home run once I dug into the details. The visual execution of the main headphone mockup fell a bit flat. The Technical Specifications menu fell into the same UX trap.

It broke down every single minor specification into its own individual row. Having to manually click and expand a drawer just to read a single one-line spec felt frustrating. Much like GPT-5.6, Grok struggled to give the ‘You may also like’ accessories grid the polish it deserved.

On the flip side, Grok nailed the footer design. The dark background, compact padding, sharp columns, and clean newsletter form looked like they were straight from an Apple or Nothing storefront.

Despite some minor struggles, Grok 4.6 delivered a cleaner visual hierarchy and much better text proportions than GPT-5.6.

Claude Code kept shipping broken code until I added this one automation

I just needed to add one hook.

By  Anurag Singh

Claude Opus 5

Thoughtful UX and the clear winner of micro-polish

Right off the bat, Claude implemented a sticky, translucent header that stayed neatly anchored as I scrolled down the page. Being able to jump between sections effortlessly without manually scrolling all the way back to the top gave it the polish of a commercial production site.

Unlike Grok’s endless clicking chores or GPT’s repetitive text, Claude found the sweet spot in the Technical Specifications menu. It presented key spec highlights upfront in a clean overview and used accordions to expand into crisp, one-sentence explanations that added value.

In the reviews section, Claude was the only model smart enough to include a clean ‘Read All Reviews’ action button alongside the rating distribution breakdown. The ‘You may also like’ section looked fantastic. The products are neatly designed compared to GPT and Grok.

It wasn’t entirely flawless, though. Much like Grok, Claude’s generated placeholder art for the main headphones felt a bit off. Also, when I toggled over to the ‘Travel Bundle’ configuration, the dynamic total price failed to recalculate and stayed at $449.

Despite that minor pricing glitch, Claude Opus 5 came away as the clear winner.

One got the design right

Any flagship AI can generate a working web page, but the real differences show up when it turns a strict design brief into a refined user experience. GPT-5.6 got the code working fast, but failed on basic typography.

Grok 4.6 brought great speed and sharp visuals, yet tripped over small details. Ultimately, Opus 5 won by focusing on what matters most in a real website: sticky navigation, thoughtful layout choices, and micro-details.

item.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Astra as the start of what it hopes will be its "AGI era"
item.itunes:title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Astra as the start of what it hopes will be its "AGI era"
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • OpenAI unveils GPT-6 Astra: most capable model, rated "Critical" for cybersecurity.
  • OpenAI explains that GPT-6 Astra is also the safest and most secure model it has made.
  • OpenAI says Astra is more robust and safer than GPT-5.6 Sol, and may usher in the AGI era.

Today has been a wild day for AI news. Earlier today, we saw Nvidia announce that it's acquiring Hugging Face for a cool $12.93 billion, promising to keep the open-source nature of the platform alive. Now, OpenAI has revealed GPT-6 Astra, the model the company hopes will deliver AGI to everyone

OpenAI pulls back the curtain on GPT-6 Astra

Plus, everything it's doing to keep it from flying off the rails

You can check out all the details of GPT-6 Astra on its system card. OpenAI calls it "the most capable model we have ever broadly deployed," and, somewhat scarily, it's the first AI model to reach "Critical " level when it comes to cybersecurity capability. OpenAI explains what that means in more tangible terms:

"This means that, with the right tools and access, GPT-6 Astra can find previously unknown security flaws and develop new ways to exploit them across many well-protected systems without a person guiding each step. Accordingly, we significantly strengthened our protections against the model taking harmful cyber actions, whether that’s due to misuse or misalignment."

While OpenAI is keen to show off how mighty its new model is, a considerable amount of the first section is dedicated to the company telling us how it'll keep it from breaking out. It says GPT-6 Astra is "significantly more robust than its predecessors," which means it's a lot harder for people to crack it open and tell it to do things against the terms of use. It's also "better aligned than GPT-5.6 Sol," which means it will keep itself more aligned with OpenAI's safety rules than its prior model. Overall, OpenAI claims that GPT-6 Astra is "significantly safer" than GPT-5.6 Sol in high-risk situations, which is reassuring to hear, given how mighty this new model seems to be.

OpenAI seems to believe that this model will be the one to achieve the legendary goal of reaching Artificial General Intelligence, or AGI. This is when an AI begins working and thinking like a human, and has been the holy grail for AI companies ever since LLMs hit the scene. In an interview reported by Wired, OpenAI President and cofounder Greg Brockman says he feels pretty confident:

“It’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era. I think that if we fast-forward a couple of years, when we look back and say, ‘When was it really that AGI was created?’ I think it's going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model."

item.title: UGREEN's new smart home platform keeps your AI and storage local, no cloud required
item.itunes:title: UGREEN's new smart home platform keeps your AI and storage local, no cloud required
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • HomeAgent merges local storage, AI, security, and device control into a single smart-home hub.
  • MasterAgent MA100 uses Nvidia Jetson Thor for heavy local AI, runs larger models and developer extensions.
  • Local-first design emphasizes privacy and on-device searches, while some cloud services remain optional.

UGREEN is moving well beyond chargers, docks, and network-attached storage. At its Smart Living Launch Event at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, which I attended on Sept. 1, the company introduced HomeAgent, a new smart home platform built around local storage and AI processing. This marks UGREEN’s first serious foray into AIoT, and the scope is broader than I expected. The lineup ranges from compact HomeAgent hubs to security cameras, a smart speaker, smart displays, and a much more powerful Nvidia Jetson-based system.

UGREEN wants HomeAgent to become your smart home's local brain

The HA100 combines storage, AI, security, and device control

  • Credit: Source: UGREEN
  • Credit: Source: UGREEN

The HomeAgent HA100 and HA100 Pro are the center of the ecosystem and the products that make UGREEN's overall pitch easiest to understand. Instead of treating local storage, smart home control, and AI as separate components, HomeAgent combines them into a single box. Files, photos, security footage, and device activity can all be stored locally, while supported AI processing also happens on the device. UGREEN says the core storage, file management, security, and smart home functions can operate over the local network without a monthly storage fee.

Building a local smart home is easy until you try to replace the speaker

I replaced everything with local-only hardware, but this was the most difficult.

4
By  Rich Edmonds

That matters because this isn't being positioned as just another Matter hub with a few extra features attached. The HA100 is designed to handle storage, security, computing, and device control together, giving UGREEN a very different starting point from companies that began with bulbs, plugs, or cameras. Matter support enables compatible devices to be integrated into a single system, allowing users to build automation scenes and coordinate multiple devices. It can also search recorded security footage using keywords, which is the kind of feature that makes local AI more useful than simply slapping an "AI" label on the box.

UGREEN is also bringing its Uliya voice assistant into the platform. Uliya can control supported devices, check live status or event history, and create voice notifications for things such as a package arriving or a baby crying. The HA100 Pro takes that further with faster networking and improved AI performance, including advanced recognition, contextual device control, and voice-based automation rule creation. That's where the distinction between the regular and Pro models starts to become more meaningful than a basic performance bump.

MasterAgent pushes UGREEN's local AI plans much further

Nvidia's Jetson Thor gives the MA100 serious processing power

The MasterAgent MA100 is where UGREEN's ambitions get much bigger. The company describes it as an agentic AI local hub built around Nvidia's Jetson Thor T5000 platform, with up to 2,070 FP4 TFLOPS of local compute performance. That's far beyond what most people would expect from a conventional smart-home hub, making the MA100 feel less like an accessory and more like a dedicated local AI appliance.

UGREEN says the added performance will let MasterAgent run larger models locally, understand more complex context and intent, and coordinate multiple devices and tasks around the home. Developers will also be able to extend it with packages or skills. That developer angle is important because a box this powerful makes more sense if UGREEN can build a broader software ecosystem around it rather than limiting it to a fixed set of first-party functions.

The rest of the announced hardware fills out the devices around those hubs. UGREEN showed the SynCare Indoor Cam ID500 Pro, SynCare PoE Cam OD600 Pro, SynCare Battery Cam OD800 Pro, Smart Speaker for Uliya, and UGREEN Gallery. Gallery includes LCD smart frames that can display photos and AI-generated highlight videos from a user's local library. Taken together, the lineup makes it clear that UGREEN isn’t testing the smart-home market with a single standalone device. It's trying to launch the pieces of an ecosystem at once.

UGREEN is betting that local AI can differentiate its ecosystem

Privacy and useful automation are central to the pitch

The part of UGREEN's strategy I find most interesting is that local processing isn't treated as a side feature. It's the foundation of the system. HomeAgent can recognize people, vehicles, pets, and packages, summarize events, surface unusual activity, and search through recorded footage. At the same time, the same platform can work with personal photos and videos stored at home. That's a much more practical use of local AI than simply adding another chatbot to a smart-home app.

The part of UGREEN's strategy I find most interesting is that local processing isn't being treated as a side feature.

There are still cloud dependencies, and UGREEN is explicit about that. Account registration and authentication, remote access, mobile notifications, software updates, and optional cloud-enabled services may still require an internet connection or cloud services. So "local-first" shouldn't be read as "completely offline." The important distinction is that UGREEN is keeping core storage, device control, and supported AI workloads in-home rather than making cloud processing the default for everything.

The launch also expands UGREEN's existing relationship with the New England Patriots. The company named Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez its Global Brand Ambassador after becoming the team's Official Tech Accessory Partner earlier this year. "Just like UGREEN, I believe great technology should help people stay prepared, reach their potential, and bring their A-game in the moments that matter most," Gonzalez said during the announcement.

Preorders for the HomeAgent HA100, HA100 Pro, and MasterAgent MA100 open Sept.3 through UGREEN's AIoT store, ahead of a Kickstarter campaign scheduled for Oct. 27. Customers can place a deposit of $50 to secure the Super Early Bird price, advertised at 50% off. Additional AIoT accessories are expected to join the campaign when it launches. The bigger question now isn't whether UGREEN wants into the smart-home market. It's whether this local-first approach can give people a reason to build around HomeAgent instead of adding yet another disconnected hub to what they already have.

item.title: I turned my old Galaxy phone into a gaming PC with Samsung DeX and one hidden feature
item.itunes:title: I turned my old Galaxy phone into a gaming PC with Samsung DeX and one hidden feature
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Consumer hardware is getting more expensive by the day due to rising AI demand and the enormous amount of compute it requires. Resources such as RAM are becoming increasingly scarce for consumers, so we have to make the most of the hardware we already have.

I've already been trying to make the most of an old laptop I had lying around, turning it into one of the most important devices in my home. I also had an old Samsung Galaxy S21 FE lying around, which is now nearly five years old. I wanted to do something useful with the smartphone and eventually turned it into a gaming beast.

"Beast" is a strong word for a mid-premium smartphone, but when I paired the Galaxy S21 FE with Samsung's DeX and Game Native and connected it to a TV, it actually lived up to that description.

The Samsung Galaxy gaming setup

Never thought I'd write these words

Samsung DeX already lets you connect a compatible Galaxy phone to a television and use Android apps through a desktop-style interface. GameNative adds the more interesting part by allowing Windows games from Steam, Epic Games, and GOG to run locally on the phone.

GameNative relies on several translation layers before a Windows game can run on Android. It uses Wine or Proton to run Windows applications, and a CPU translator to convert x86 or x64 instructions for the phone's ARM processor. Tools such as DXVK or VKD3D then translate DirectX graphics calls into Vulkan. The Galaxy GPU renders the final image, and DeX displays it on the television.

I was able to run the setup comfortably on the Galaxy S21 FE, which means it should also run well on any newer Galaxy S series and Z series phones. The phone also needs a USB-C dock because its single port has to handle HDMI output, power, and wired accessories simultaneously. You are also going to need a 45W or 65W PPS charger and, if you really want to make the most of this setup, an Xbox controller, a PlayStation controller, or another compatible XInput controller.

The Pixel's desktop mode feels like a real operating system, and it's already better than I expected

I don't know when I'd actually use the Pixel's desktop mode, but it's surprisingly polished despite its lackluster third-party app support.

6
By  Patrick O'Rourke

Setting up DeX and getting the performance right

This takes some effort

For gaming, a wired DeX connection is the better option because wireless DeX adds compression and input delay. I connected a charger to the USB-C dock, ran HDMI from the dock to the TV, and then plugged in the Galaxy S21 FE. I kept DeX at 1920×1080 pixels and 60Hz, since pushing 4K only adds more load and many docks or TVs drop to 30Hz at that resolution.

The TV also needs Game Mode enabled, with motion smoothing and other image-processing features turned off to reduce latency. Once DeX is running, the phone's display can stay off. In Game Booster, I used the Performance profile. On supported devices, the optional "Pause USB PD charging when gaming" setting can also help reduce heat by limiting battery charging during gameplay.

For GameNative, 1280 × 720 at 30fps is a good starting point for demanding games on the S21 FE. You can push lighter titles to higher resolutions once they are stable. I would only change the renderer, graphics driver, or DirectX wrapper if a game has compatibility or performance issues. LSFG frame generation can make a stable 30 fps output look closer to 60 fps, but it works best as a finishing touch after the game is already running smoothly.

How well does it actually run games?

It's pretty impressive

My Galaxy S21 FE is the Snapdragon 888 model with 8GB of RAM, and the results were better than I expected from a phone this old.

It goes without saying that this setup really shines in lighter games. For example, Dead Cells runs extremely well and is almost ideal for something like this because it already works perfectly with a controller and doesn't put much pressure on the hardware. Portal 2 was another surprisingly good experience. Once you're sitting on the couch with the game running through DeX on a television, it doesn't feel like you're playing a Windows game on an old Android phone.

However, titles such as The Witcher 3, Cyberpunk 2077, and Red Dead Redemption 2 push the Snapdragon 888 to its limits, so this is where you can lower the resolution and target a stable 30fps. You're obviously not getting the same experience as with a modern gaming PC or console, but the fact that games of this scale can run locally on the S21 FE at all makes the setup impressive.

Heat is the biggest issue I encountered – the S21 FE already has a reputation for running hot, and my unit has heated up considerably even during normal use over the years, so gaming only makes things worse.

I wouldn't use the S21 FE as a replacement for a gaming PC or console. But for an old phone that was otherwise sitting idle, being able to play Dead Cells, Portal 2, and even experiment with games like Cyberpunk 2077 on a television gives it a remarkably useful second life.

The future of Android-powered TV streaming sticks looks uncertain

The Google TV Streamer was released in 2024 and the future of something new isn't clear.

4
By  Brian Burgess

I don't mind carrying portable SSDs, but sometimes I don't need that much space, and they can become a burden when you're trying to stay extremely lightweight. That's where a USB flash drive like the one from Verbatim comes in handy. It's simple, sleek, and does the job.

item.title: I used Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini to build a resume, but only one felt interview-ready
item.itunes:title: I used Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini to build a resume, but only one felt interview-ready
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
While some people use AI to write entire documents or completely replace their work, this opens you up to problems like hallucinations and generic output. The real value of AI tools lies in using them as collaborative partners that can help you identify blind spots and speed up repetitive processes.

So recently, when a friend needed help with the resume, but both of us were struggling with the planning stage, I decided to try out Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini to get some insights on how to approach the document.

I gave Claude Code control of my desktop for a week, and it automated things I didn't think were possible

I was seriously stunned.

59
By  Simon Batt

Why use AI for help with a resume?

Leveraging AI's strengths while retaining control

In this particular scenario, AI was the perfect tool to help me craft the resume. My friend has some old experience as a paramedic and currently works in sales. item.title: 10 GbE finally stopped being an enterprise-only luxury, and a single PCIe card is all it takes to prove it
item.itunes:title: 10 GbE finally stopped being an enterprise-only luxury, and a single PCIe card is all it takes to prove it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Let's face it, my home network has been embarrassing for a while. There's a Synology DS1621xs+ in the rack with a 10 GbE port that came out of the box, and until last month it had spent its entire life plugged into a switch that topped out at 2.5 GbE, which is its own kind of bottleneck nobody warns you about when you upgrade a NAS to 10 Gigabit. My desktop wasn't any better: the MSI MPG X870E Carbon WiFi has a 5 GbE port onboard that has never once negotiated 5 GbE, because nothing else in the house speaks it. I'd built a lab full of multi-gig hardware and connected it with what amounts to a slightly faster Gigabit.

The fix was a used Dell-branded Mellanox card off eBay that cost about the same as the cable I plugged into it. And the thing is, this isn't a story about a good deal. It's a story about a market that flipped when nobody was looking, because a 10GbE network card went from something you budgeted for to something you buy with the change from a RAM upgrade. Three things changed at once, and the switch, which everyone assumes is the expensive part, is the least interesting of them.

HBA cards unlock cheap enterprise storage for your NAS, but the gotchas are real

HBAs come with their own quirks when installed in consumer-grade hardware, but they're well worth your while

1
By  Ty Sherback

The PCIe card is the cheap part now

I picked up my ex-data center card for less than lunch money

The PCIe card I picked up was the Dell Mellanox CX4121C, a dual-SFP28 port card capable of 25 GbE. It runs over PCIe 3.0 x8, cost me $27 shipped, and used listings currently are a few dollars higher, but not by much. It's the networking equivalent of buying last-gen Xeon boards, because the data centers all moved to 100 GbE and beyond, so all the 10 GbE hardware got scrapped.

I don't need the 25 GbE capability yet, but it'll negotiate fine at 10 GbE, and that's perfect for my current needs. I noticed a ton of Intel X540-T2 cards while I was browsing, but Proxmox forum users say they run hot and don't get the full speed, so the Mellanox cards are going to be a better option.

Mellanox ConnectX-4

The ConnectX-4 is a 10/25 GbE PCIe networking card that can be picked up for pennies on the original cost, thanks to the data center market moving to even faster cards.

Your operating system now has the drivers

No more weird driver shenanigans for many 10 GbE cards

Price was never the thing keeping these PCIe cards out of desktop PCs, because they've stayed around the same price since eBay got flooded with them. But driver support was abysmal, and you had to download a vendor file, flash the firmware, and find a five-year-old forum post that had the steps to get it running.

But you don't need that anymore for Windows 11, because Nvidia's WinOF-2 driver is shipped for the ConnectX-4 to ConnectX-6 family. That's certainly been the case with my ConnectX-4 card, which installed with no issues after a quick reboot. It wasn't completely painless, though, as a copper DAC cable refused to negotiate a link with the switch, and I had to spend $20 on a Brocade active optical cable to get the link working.

Oh, and that's why you skip the $20 ConnectX-3 cards that are also all over eBay and other secondhand hardware vendors. There's no in-box Windows driver, and getting it working is a pain.

Please stop using third-party drivers update utilities

Most driver update utilities are just bloatware

12
By  Tom Li

Realtek made the RJ45 route cheap

Now you can get 10 GbE for under $50

If you'd rather stick with RJ45 ports and not buy new cables, Realtek's RTL8127 is the low-cost option, and you can pick up a PCIe card with one and 10 GbE speeds for under $50. It uses under 2W of power, runs on a single PCIe 4.0 lane, and the Linux kernel got driver support in version 6.16.

Before that, cards using the Marvell AQC113 were the lowest-priced to enter, and they were around $70 when launched. The only issue with using 10GBASE-T is heat, because an average port uses 2 to 5W, compared to less than one watt for SFP+. I use an SFP+ to RJ45 adapter to connect to my NAS because Synology charges $200+ for a compatible SFP+ add-in card, but I'd be lying if it stayed cool when used.

RJ45 vs. SFP: Which network interface should you use?

Having a hard time choosing the ideal port for your networking needs? We're here to help out!

2
By  Ayush Pande

A managed switch is where the money goes

Which is why SFP+ matters for your hardware

A $50 10 GbE PCIe NIC is a great thing to have, but if you have nothing to plug it into, you're just indulging in retail therapy. And that's where math stops making sense again, because a 10 GbE switch is still $150+, or closer to twice that for a name you recognize.

But most home users don't need eight 10 GbE ports, or even five. I have dozens of machines in my office, and only two things that hold data regularly use 10 GbE: my desktop PC and my NAS. My home server also has 10 GbE, but it's not always turned on to save electricity, and it's booted up only for heavy tasks.

A $30 managed switch does what your $300 gaming router can't

I stopped trusting gaming routers for traffic management after learning what a managed switch actually does.

3
By  Jasmine Mannan

The market wants you on 5 GbE

Then it can sell you 10 GbE later on, as well

Here's the thing. The consumer market has barely decided to sell 2.5 GbE equipment, whether that's PC motherboards, mini PCs, routers, or network switches. They don't want to jump straight to 10 GbE across everything, because there's a 5 GbE stepping stone along the way. The only segment that disagreed was the NAS makers, who went straight from 1 GbE to 10 GbE. There's a fair case that 2.5GbE was the right choice all along for most homes, and I don't disagree. Just not for the two machines that actually move files.

Onboard 10 GbE does exist, but only when you get into the prosumer and top-end motherboards. I couldn't find one under $400 with it, and the closest is probably the Asus X870e ProArt. So your choices are between an expensive motherboard that you might upgrade when the next CPU generation comes out, or a relatively inexpensive PCIe card that can work with many future PCs.

I connected my NAS directly to my PC with 10 gigabit Ethernet, and skipped upgrading the rest of my network

You don't necessarily need a 10G switch to get blazing-fast transfer speeds between your PC and NAS

13
By  Ayush Pande

Your next 10 GbE upgrade has already been paid for by the enterprise market

Add it up: a used ConnectX-4 Lx for $26 to $50, an SFP+ cable for $20, and a two-port SFP+ switch for $120 that you buy once. The NAS port that's been sitting idle since the day you unboxed it finally has a partner, and the whole thing plugs in and works on Windows 11 without a driver download. Three years ago, 10 GbE at home meant a fan-cooled switch, an Intel card that could cook an egg, and a driver with a known-issues list longer than this article.

You still have to make some decisions. You pick SFP+ over copper or pay the heat tax on 10GBASE-T, and you accept that two fast ports is the whole upgrade rather than a rack full of them. But if you've got a NAS with a 10GbE port and a PC with a spare PCIe slot, the cheapest thing you can do for your home network right now is stop waiting for the motherboard makers and buy the card the data center threw away.

There's a Synology DS1621xs+ in the rack with a 10 GbE port that came out of the box, and until last month it had spent its entire life plugged into a switch that topped out at 2.5 GbE, which is its own kind of bottleneck nobody warns you about when you upgrade a NAS to 10 Gigabit. I'd built a lab full of multi-gig hardware and connected it with what amounts to a slightly faster Gigabit.

The fix was a used Dell-branded Mellanox card off eBay that cost about the same as the cable I plugged into it. And the thing is, this isn't a story about a good deal. It's a story about a market that flipped when nobody was looking, because a 10GbE network card went from something you budgeted for to something you buy with the change from a RAM upgrade. Three things changed at once, and the switch, which everyone assumes is the expensive part, is the least interesting of them.

1

item.title: My cheapest SSD is doing the most important job in my PC, and that's on purpose
item.itunes:title: My cheapest SSD is doing the most important job in my PC, and that's on purpose
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
A little over five years ago, I bought a SATA SSD that, for one reason or the other, spent a frankly embarrassing amount of time doing absolutely nothing. It was unboxed and sitting in a drawer for years. Eventually, I found it again, wired it into my PC, and gave it a purpose, which I should've done long ago.

Over the next few months, the 250GB Crucial BX500 changed how my PC's storage worked in tandem, simply by doing three jobs that my PCIe Gen 4 NVMe was never the right fit for. Suffice it to say, my cheap SATA drive is a little more than just a 250-gig storage expansion, and it makes my NVMe a lot happier by just being installed on the same system. Here's why.

Windows' pagefile does not warrant a Gen 4 NVMe

There's no need to burden the fastest drive for every workload, and it pays not to

A few days ago, I talked about moving my Windows pagefile from my PCIe Gen 4 NVMe to my SATA SSD, which happens to be common practice amongst enthusiasts, but is seldom recommended by manufacturers or OEMs. To the contrary, the advice generally is to put the pagefile on the fastest drive.

The pagefile is one of those Windows things that mostly sits in the background until your PC actually has a need for it. When the system memory is under pressure, the OS moves the less-active memory pages to pagefile.sys. On my build with 32GB of DDR5, this is a rare occurrence in my day-to-day activity, but Windows still writes crash dumps, housekeeping traffic, and kernel data to the file.

Now, that isn't something a modern NVMe notices. The problem is the pagefile isn't the only workload that's handled by the primary boot drive. The OS keeps the drive busy with updates, background telemetry, system logging, browser caching, file indexing, and a dozen more tasks that involve constant reads and writes. Simply moving the pagefile to a SATA SSD reduces the strain on the NVMe, and in my case, when the SATA SSD is doing mostly nothing, it benefits my NVMe by reserving its bandwidth for bursty work in the foreground.

Most of my games don't care that they're on SATA

The difference between SATA and NVMe load times is imperceptible

Another really common piece of advice that echoes in hardware circles is that all of your games always need to go on the fastest drive to deliver the best performance and load times. It sounds like the most obvious, intuitive thing to do, but even with a 2TB NVMe SSD, my game library quickly took up to 30–40% of the storage space I had, thanks to how massive AAA games have become these days.

Needless to say, this had me revisiting the available benchmarks to see if there was an actual performance or load time penalty I would be witnessing if I were to migrate a sizable chunk of my game library over to my SATA SSD. A single search later, I realized that the "penalty" I had assumed didn't really exist; at least not in the way that I thought.

In a very recent benchmark, Tom's Hardware tested SATA, PCIe 3.0, 4.0, and 5.0 SSDs across 11 storage-heavy titles to measure whether there were any notable performance differences between the four storage types, in a system running with 16GB of RAM. Out of the 11 tested, 9 showed no performance differences, and absolutely no signs of visual anomalies like texture pop-in or texture loading issues.

When you delve into the technical specifics, it all makes perfect sense. The major advantage a PCIe 4.0 M.2 NVMe has over a cheap SATA SSD isn't fully reflected in the type of workload gaming demands, as modern titles spend much of their time performing small random reads at low QDs (queue depths) rather than relying on sequential throughput. As such, there's no reason for most games to go to an NVMe SSD.

My Ollama library lives on my slowest SSD, on purpose

Constant "ollama pull" and "ollama rm" cycles are a pain for the NVMe SSD

Besides holding a huge part of my game library, the BX500 has also become my local AI model warehouse for good reason. Every single model that I use is stored on it, from the small 8B models ranging from 4 to 6 GB to the bulkier ones that ask for 15–20 GB. The reason why it works just as well comes down to how these local models use storage.

Whenever I run a model, the weights are loaded from the disk into the VRAM once, and from there, the SSD has practically no bearing on everything that happens after. Token generation speed depends entirely on my 4070 Ti Super's GDDR6X memory and compute, and has nothing to do with where the actual model files are stored.

There's also another reason for this. I'm constantly swapping older models for newer ones, which means constant ollama pull and ollama rm cycles, moving potentially hundreds of gigabytes per month as I rotate models. Routing the entire library to SATA essentially means the bulk of the churn is never the NVMe SSD's burden to bear.

The only thing I have to be cautious about is whether the model weights, the KV cache and compute buffer all fit neatly into the VRAM so that the tokens/second isn't affected, but that's something I'd have to ascertain regardless of where the model files are situated.

My NVMe SSD lives easier because of my SATA SSD

Having more than one storage device on your PC is always a great thing, but it's also important to revisit the division of labor (or perhaps I should say, storage) sometimes. My BX500 spent an unreasonable amount of its life doing absolutely nothing, but a few hours of migrating a few files and adjusting Windows settings made it a place where I can host my game library, my local AI models, and the pagefile, while my Gen 4 NVMe gets to breathe easy, live longer, and work only on tasks that justify its throughput.

item.itunes:title: Claude is an okay ChatGPT alternative, this AI tool is better than both
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
For most people looking beyond ChatGPT, Claude usually feels like the obvious choice. Anthropic has nailed the fundamentals, and it easily gives OpenAI a run for its money.

But sticking to the two usual suspects means you might be missing where the real momentum is actually happening: xAI's Grok 4.6. Over the last few months, Grok has quietly evolved into a genuine powerhouse. If you want a tool that outworks both in daily practice, it's time to pay attention to Grok 4.6.

Why Claude couldn't close the gap

Missing image tools and sluggish research

When I decided to step away from ChatGPT, Claude was naturally the first place I landed. It felt like a sensible, grown-up upgrade. But it didn't take long for the cracks to show in my everyday setup. The biggest immediate roadblock was image generation. In ChatGPT, knocking out a quick Instagram banner, a blog thumbnail, or visualizing an asset happens right inside the chat. With Claude, that workflow hit a wall.

After all, I don't want to switch to another app to create a few images for my social media accounts. Then came the research problem. Claude is a brilliant conversationalist, but it often misses the tone. Besides, I didn't want to go back to ChatGPT's robotic tone.

That's when I started looking for alternatives and came across Grok.

Tone, usability, and practical output

No fluff

One of the most exhausting parts of using ChatGPT and Claude is the endless prompt micromanagement. The real daily test of any AI model isn't benchmark scores; it's how much time you spend getting a decent answer out of it. With ChatGPT and Claude, my prompt history is full of extra instructions I had to set manually: "keep it concise," "don't give me a summary," or "skip the preamble." If you don't micromanage them, you usually end up with several paragraphs of corporate fluff or an essay you never asked for.

With Grok, the difference in tone was obvious on day one. Its responses get straight to the point without sounding like a robotic press release or an overly apologetic assistant. It answers in natural, straightforward English. Most importantly, it just saves me time. I am not stuck playing prompt engineer, writing three follow-up messages to trim down an explanation or fix tone issues. You ask a direct question, and you get a direct, practical answer on the first pass.

Excellent coding capabilities

Just try out Grok in Cursor

Grok earned a permanent spot in my setup due to Cursor. I spend a huge chunk of my week writing and debugging code, and the editor integration is usually where an AI either proves its worth or gets stuck to basic chat queries. It's not as effective as something like Fable 5 for hyper-complex edge cases. During my direct comparisons, Grok 4.6 often came second to Claude Code. However, compared to Codex, it's quite fast and uses fewer tokens.

I like how Grok doesn't stretch its suggestions with unnecessary comments or rewrite entire files when I only asked to touch a single function. I highly underestimated Grok's coding capabilities, but after trying it out in Cursor, I came away impressed.

Robust media generation tools

Very important for my workflow

If you use Claude, your media generation options begin and end with text. There is no image generation, let alone motion. When I needed visuals, I kept Midjourney open in another tab. With Grok, visual creation is baked directly into the conversation. It handles photos like a pro, but the feature that blew me away is the short-form video generation. I can request a still image and animate it into a tight, cinematic clip right in the same thread.

I was drafting copy for a mock tech-accessory campaign – a matte-black wireless charging puck. I typed:

A matte-black wireless charging pad sitting on a dark oak desk, with warm ambient lighting in the background. Close-up macro shot.

And in seconds, I had a crisp still. Instead of stopping there, I used Grok's video tool to animate it. A slow, cinematic camera pan glides left to right around the charger. Subtle reflections shift across the aluminum ring, with a shallow depth of field. There's even an option to turn any image into a video using the play button.

Grok Bot looks promising

Where it still falls short

The Grok Bot really excites me. Instead of babysitting a chat tab, an autonomous agent handles repetitive web tasks in the background. I have yet to test it through, but I can't wait to integrate it into my workflow.

Still, Grok isn't perfect. It lacks the polish of Claude's Artifacts for live previews, and for creative long-form writing, Claude still sounds more natural and less dry. It also needs to work on releasing a native desktop app for Windows and Mac. Both Claude and ChatGPT are way ahead with their native offerings.

Real-world power without the fuss

ChatGPT will always have brand recognition, and Claude remains a reliable coding partner for complex tasks. But between them, Grok is the one that's rapidly improving and gets the job done for my workflow.

With Grok 4.7 just around the corner, I can't wait to see what the team brings to the table. Next time you hit a wall drafting complex logic or sifting through breaking technical data, skip your default browser bookmarks and take Grok 4.6 for a spin.

Grok

Grok is an AI tool that rivals Gemini, ChatGPT, and Claude.

item.title: Microsoft reduces Xbox Cloud Gaming playtime to a measly 15 hours a month a year after full rollout
item.itunes:title: Microsoft reduces Xbox Cloud Gaming playtime to a measly 15 hours a month a year after full rollout
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Xbox Cloud Gaming gets monthly caps: Ultimate 15h, Premium 10h, Essential 5h starting in November.
  • Only ~4% affected, but heavy users must buy extra hours via the Xbox Store; pricing and regional rules unknown.
  • Limits aim to curb PC hogging as cloud demand rises, risking loss to rivals like GeForce Now.

A year ago, we saw the Xbox Cloud Gaming service roll out to all tiers of the Xbox Game Pass. The Ultimate tier had access to it for years prior, so it was a nice surprise. Now, Microsoft is bringing another surprise, although it's not a nice one. Xbox Game Pass Ultimate subscribers can only play on the Cloud Gaming service for 15 hours a month, and that's the high end of the limitation.

Xbox Game Pass gets a new monthly limit, and it doesn't look pretty

Xbox Game Pass Essential subscribers are especially down on their luck

On the Xbox News website, Microsoft has announced new changes to its Cloud Gaming service. If you're an avid user of it, you only have a few months of use until these pretty nasty time restrictions are placed on your account:

Beginning in November, we’re changing how cloud gaming is included with XBOX Game Pass.

Game Pass plans will include a set number of cloud gaming hours each month:

  • Game Pass Ultimate: 15 hours
  • Game Pass Premium: 10 hours
  • Game Pass Essential: 5 hours

Today, eligible Game Pass subscribers can stream without these monthly hour limits.

Microsoft says that this change should only affect "4% of Game Pass subscribers," but it's still a pretty huge impact for that 4%, even for the highest-paying tier.

So, what happens when you run out of hours? Well, Microsoft states that you can buy more time via the Xbox Store. The company wasn't ready to reveal how much people will need to pay per hour, or if people on the higher tiers will get a discount, but it did say that "Available hours, purchasing options, and cloud gaming features" will vary by region.

Microsoft claims it's making this move due to people using the Cloud Gaming service more often and for longer than ever before. As such, Microsoft wants to put these restrictions in place to stop people hogging the PCs. It runs the risk of losing business to its cloud gaming competitors, especially given how Nvidia GeForce Now brought "PC-quality" game performance to Amazon Fire TV Sticks.

I ditched my gaming PC for cloud gaming when hardware prices spiraled out of control

It's not perfect, but it's a solution.
